caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 257 of 1980.
lawyer:
M.I. Farooqui ----- For Appellant
Ismailuddin Sarkar Asst. Attorney General ----- For Respondent
parties:
Mrs. Rana Awan ----- Appellant
vs.
Govt. of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The judgment-debtor alleged that the Suit decree holder obtained a decree in Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 for realization of the rental compensation from the judgment-debtor for a house under the control and management of the judgment debtor as abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The decree-holder obtained an expert decree and filed money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 for recovery of the decretal amount. 

 5. According to Mr. Farooqui, this barring provision has no application in the fact of the instant case. Since the decision in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1975 clearly concluded the question whether the action of the Government was protected within the meaning and scope of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In the said Writ Petition an objection was raised in justification of the action taken by the Government while treating the disputed property as an abandoned property. The High Court "Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh held "that action of the Government treating the Petitioner's house as all abandoned property is without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to make over possession of the house to the petitioner at once." 

 6. It is admitted that in terms of the aforesaid decision in Writ Petition, the Government made over possession of the disputed property to the petitioner. Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 was filed for recovery of the amount of rent received by the Government during the period of its control and management. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 7.3.78. Thereafter, Money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 was started for recovery of the decretal dues. The objection under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure aimed at a question to oust the jurisdiction of the Court so far as the money suit was concerned. According to the Government, the learned Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and to pass the decree in view of the bar of Article 23 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Mr. Farooqui has drawn our attention to the case of Bangladeshi Steel Mills Vs. Masud Reza 30 D.L.R. (SC) 169 for the proposition that if the property does not answer the description of abandoned property, no occasion arises for application of the abandoned property order. We have already referred to the judgment of this Court in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1975, where it was held that "the action of the Government treating the petitioner s house as abandoned property is without lawful authority and of no legal effect." 

 7. In the case of Abdur Rauf and others Vs. Abdul Hamid Khan and others reported in 17 D.L.R 515 it has been held that the Civil Court's jurisdiction is not barred and the distinction between an Order passed under the Act or under the chapter was considered. Their Lordships noticed that civil Courts have jurisdiction as under section 9, Civil Procedure Code, to try all suits of a civil nature excepting those the trial of which is expressly or impliedly barred. The alleged action in the instant case claimed to be protected under the Act, namely under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The learned Judges of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the aforesaid case expressed this in the following words:- 

 In view of the decision-in writ petition No. 287 of 1975, it cannot be said that the order passed and action taken were under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Thus the protection of Article 23 of P.O. 16 of 1972 does not appear to be applicable in the facts of the instant case. 

 Similar view was expressed in the case of Nasiruddin Vs. Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in D.L.R. 32, 31 (AD) 216. In that case protection under M. L.R. No. 7 failed to attract the action taken in the said case. 

 9. Referring to the expression "nor shall any such taking over of vesting of property give rise to any claim to compensation", the learned Assistant Attorney General contends that the decree was without jurisdiction since the bar by Article 5 of M. L.R. No. 7 of 1977 applied to the instant case. It was not a suit for any claim of compensation but it was suit for recovery of the money received by the Government by way of rent for the relevant period. It was not receiveable by the Government on the strength of its action under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The contention of the learned Assistant Attorney General does not hold well in view of the facts of the instant case and the nature of suit. The suit was decreed ex-parte. It was not a suit for recovery of any compensation for the wrongful act nor it was the suit for mesne profits. It is evident from the materials one record that the suit was one for recovery of the amount received by the judgment debtor without any lawful authority. Such a suit does not appear to be protected under the mischief of Article 5 of M.L.R. No. 7 of 1977. 

 10. Having considered the aforesaid decision we are of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in going beyond the decree while holding that the decree was without jurisdiction. The cases referred to above may be considered in the light of the case of the Secretary of State Vs. Mask and Co. 44 C. W.N. page 709. This decision clearly applies in the facts and circumstance of the instant case. The learned Subordinate Judge did not take into consideration the principles laid down in the cases referred to above while striking down the execution case. 

 11. It has been contended by Mr. Faruqui that the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure is limited to the extent of investigation as to whether the court which passed the decree did so without jurisdiction. The illegal exercise of jurisdiction or illegality in the decision is not within the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Faruqui has referred to the case of Gora Chand Halder Vs. Prafulla Kumar Roy and others reported in 29 C.WN. page 948. In this Full Bench case it was held that "where the decree presented for execution was made by Court which apparently had no jurisdiction, whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of judgment debtor's person to make the decree the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. Within these narrow limits the executing Court is authorized to question the validity of the decree." This decision of the Full Bench appears to have been uniformly followed. Mr. Sarkar has also referred to the case of Lunatic Kumar Chanchal Kumar Ray Vs. Kumar Jagadish Ch. Singha represented by the Manager, Paik Para Raj Wards Estate reported in 6 D.L.R. Page 561. A Division Bench of the Dacca High Court considered the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and explained the aforesaid Full Bench decision in the following terms :- 

 "It is only in very exceptional cases, where on the face of the decree it is clear that the Court which passed the decree had no inherent jurisdiction to do so, that the executing Court can refuse to execute the decree, but otherwise, it is not open to the executing Court to go behind the decree and determine for itself whether the decree passed by the Court having jurisdiction is valid or not." 

 12. In the aforesaid case their Lordships of the Dacca High Court discussed a large number of decisions resting on the question. 

 13. A similar view was also taken in the case of Islamic Republic of Pakistan Vs. Mohammad Saeed reported in 13 D.L R. (S.C) page 84. Hamoodur Rahman. J, as his Lordship was then, expressed his views in the following terms:- 

 14. In the instant case, the Government judgment-debtor produced no materials before the executing Court to hold that the decree in question was passed by a Court without jurisdiction or that the decree itself was null and void or that it was incapable of execution. The illegal or improper exercise of jurisdiction or illegality of the decision are no grounds for challenging the decree under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A similar view has also been taken in a recent decision in the case of Hajee Md. Ahsanullah Vs. Arafatunnessa Bibi being dead her heirs Ali Ahmad and others in 33 D.L.R. (A.D) 17. In the case it has been held that "where the decree presented for execution was made by a Court which apparently had no jurisdiction whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of the judgment debtor's person to make the decree, the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. Within these narrow limits the executing Court is empowered to question validity of the decree." 

 15. It may be said that a decree to be without jurisdiction must be of such a nature as to make it a void decree or a nullity, In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, we have not been presented with any material to hold that the decree was void or that it was a nullity. The total absence of jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree has not been proved in the facts and circumstances of the case. Accordingly we hold that the decree was not without jurisdiction. The learned Subordinate Judge, as an executing Court, erred in law in going behind the decree. On a consideration of the aforesaid decisions we hold that the executing Court went wrong in not taking into consideration the proper scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure as authorized in law and supported by a long chain of decisions. Therefore, the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are liable to be set aside. 

 16. We have been taken through the objection petition filed by the Government under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In paragraph 4 of the objection petition it has been stated that Tk. 1,74,896/- have been paid for renovation and repair or the house in question. So the execution case cannot proceed for the entire decretal amount. The learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have directed his consideration towards the aforesaid objection. We need not say anything as to the merits or otherwise of the said objection. 

 17. For the aforesaid reasons the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and Money Execution case No. 5 of 1979 is restored to file, Miscellaneous Case No. 121 of 1979 is remitted to the Executing Court for disposal according to law and on evidence as may be adduced by the parties. 

 18. In the result the appeal succeeds and is allowed without any order as to costs. Money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 is restored to file and Miscellaneous Case No. 121 of 1979 arising out of the said Money Execution Case under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure do proceed according to law and in the light of the observations made above.
